# Style

These forms make BPL easy to read for someone who doesn't know APL. How a line reads decides between them. Resemblance to APL counts for nothing.

Use spaces to show the top-level structure of an expression. Keep parentheses where they make nested scope easier to see, as in `⍺,(↓key_val,join),⍵`. Keep connected tokens in one run. Use `⁝` (Alt-:) where tokens must stay distinct without ending the run: `h⁝m`, `+/⍠i⁝m`. Two names that touch merge, as `ix` does in `+/⍠ix`. A name followed by a literal stays separate: `f1` is `f(1)`. [Syntax](syntax.qmd#runs) gives the grouping rules.

A function between two runs takes a space on each side, as in `a×b + c`. A space on one side only changes the grouping: `a×b +c` is the strand `[a×b ; +c]`, and `a×b+ c` applies the train `a×b+` to `c`.

For a derived function with only a right argument, `⁝` separates the operand from the argument where a boundary is needed: `f⍣3⁝0`, `10÷√1++/⍠i⁝m`, `(+/÷≢)⍤1⁝2 3⍴⍳6`. It stops literal stranding without grouping the expression before it. A vector argument can touch the operand in brackets: `≥⍣2[1 2 3]`. Add nothing where tokens already stay distinct, as in `+/⍤1m` or `(+/÷≢)⍠d⊼n`.

With both a left and a right argument, parentheses around the derived function show it between them: `10 20(+⍤1)m`. Keep parentheses where a compound operand or nested train needs grouping, as in `⌊@(10×)x`.

A space groups the whole run before it, including any prefix. `+/÷≢ ⊼y-c+h+.×v` applies the mean train to its complete argument. `mean_square←+/÷≢ ⊼` separates an atop's subtrains. `f⁝g⁝h x` keeps three named functions in one run. `+/÷≢⁝v` doesn't group the mean train. For nested parentheses, try removing the inner pair first: `(+⌿ N*Ms ÷ ≢N)*÷Ms`. Naming a train that a line uses twice can read better: `mean⍤1m`.

Lowercase `j` reads most clearly in complex literals, as in `3j4`. Uppercase `J` is an input alias, and only its own tests need it. Archived upstream source keeps its original form. Array notation shows a literal matrix's rows directly, as in `[10 20 30⋄40 50 60]`, where a reshape hides them. A reshape still suits an example about reshape. A `⋄` between rows reads best with no spaces around it. A `⋄` between statements reads best with a space on each side.

Brackets build a list from names or expressions. A bare literal list, such as `1 2 3`, is a shorthand. In brackets, a list of names reads as a list at a glance, as in `[a b]`, even where `a b` would also work. `[n 2]⍴0`, `[x],y`, `[a⋄b]` and `f⍤1 m` read more directly than APL's `(n,2)⍴0`, `(⊂x),y`, `⊃[a b]` and `⊃f¨↓m`. Where no item of a bracket list contains a space, spaces separate the items more lightly than `;`: `[i j]` rather than `[i;j]`.

An operand often reads best touching its operator, with parentheses around a compound operand, as in `⌊@(10×)x` and `(≢⊢)⌸x`. Spacing also makes a run into an operand: after a dyadic operator and a space, the whole next run is the operand, as in `⌊@ 10× x`. When both operands are compound, parentheses around each show the grouping: `(•ucs 9)@(⍸tabs)⍵`. An operand keeps its parentheses when a left argument comes before it, as in `tree (⍺⍢)/ next`. Report any case where none of these forms reads well.

A train reads more directly than naming an argument twice: `+/÷≢ v` rather than `+/v ÷ ≢v`. A tacit form usually reads more directly than a dfn. A dfn reads better where the tacit form would be longer or clearly awkward.

`fib10` means `fib 10`, not an identifier, which would be `fib_10`. That form reads well where it's shorter and needs no new parentheses. `32•float∞` converts `∞` to a 32-bit float, as `32 •float ∞` does with spaces it doesn't need. `32 •float∞` gives the two items `32 64ₓ` instead: the runs `32` and `•float∞` strand, and `•float∞` alone gives ∞'s width. When spaces separate names in a dyadic call, keep both: `x f 5` rather than `x f5`.

`⌷` reads clearly for a selection, as in `[⍋v]⌷v`. A subscript reads best for one literal position, as in `v₁` and `v₁←0`. `.` suits other assignment targets, such as `v.[i]←0`, record fields, such as `T.name`, and places where `⌷` would be longer. A target that is a cross product of positions takes `⌷` with a spaced `←`, as in `[1 3;0 5]⌷a +←10`. `.` pairs its index arrays instead: `a.[1 3;0 5]` selects only the items at positions 1 0 and 3 5.

Positions and counts are exact, while bare numbers are floats. Arithmetic that mixes the two gives floats. Under dynamic kinds, a write that mixes them leaves the array in mixed storage. `⍳10ₓ` and `⍳≢x` give exact positions, where `⍳10` gives floats. An array that will hold positions or counts stays exact when it starts from exact numbers, as in `n⍴¯1ₓ`, with a counter starting at `0ₓ`. On positions, `≥i`, `i+1ₓ` and `2ₓ×i` stay exact, where `i+1` and `2×i` give floats. For an exact `v`, `+/÷≢ v` gives an exact rational. `+/÷1×≢ v` gives a float. Where a map's branches give Booleans and numbers, converting the Boolean gives one type: `+b` gives exact integers, and `1×b` gives floats.
